title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
purpose: It sets out the duties of affection owed to fellow believers, parents, kin, and neighbors, drawing on the sayings of Ali ibn Abi Talib, the Mustansiriya councils, and a juristic question-and-answer, and shows how each duty divides into obligatory parts and accompanying manners.

points.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib, in his four hundred manners, warns believers not to despise weak brothers (whoever despises a believer is belittled and detested by God and will not be joined with him on the Day of Resurrection unless he repents), not to force a brother to ask when his need is already known, and to visit, be tender, and give freely rather than be like the hypocrite who describes what he does not do.

Ali is quoted as saying the Muslim is the mirror of his Muslim brother, so that a brother's slip is met with guidance, counsel and gentleness rather than a group banding against him, and discord is condemned because it leads a person away from the path.

Ali forbids backbiting on the authority of the Qur'anic rebuke 'Would any of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother?', and urges that meeting believers with a handshake and a bright face causes the burdens each carried to lift by the time they part.

A recorded question from Shaykh Shimon bin Muhammad al-Ghuri al-Hindi about the Indian custom of asking neighbors for water, salt and food when one lacks them at the moment (though able to buy) was answered by Sayyidina Hassan bin Idris bin al-Hassan bin Abdullah al-Ala: there is no harm in it, since it belongs to the purity of affection and the excellence of brotherhood.

In the seventeenth Mustansiriya council, righteousness toward parents is named the first of the twelve practices that correspond to the number of the letters of the testimony, the seven obligatory rights corresponding to its seven clauses having already been explained.

From the two Qur'anic verses enjoining goodness toward both parents, the council draws the point that in both places it is the mother's deed alone (carrying in hardship, weakness upon weakness) that is laid to the child's account, so she whom God distinguished by mention must be distinguished with honor and righteousness.

The eighteenth council divides righteousness toward parents into seven obligatory parts and twelve manners, and identifies three pairs of parents: the bodily parents who caused his form to come into being and nourished him, the two parents in religion who caused his form in knowledge (the Imam of the age and his proof), and the two fathers of the community who convey the divine sciences (the Prophet and the legatee, and the Imams of their progeny), citing 'I and you, O Ali, are the two fathers of this community.'

The seal of righteousness toward parents is a person's righteousness toward his own soul: making the truth plain to it and establishing it therein, magnifying it so as to awaken its longing, placing fear in it, dealing gently with it, delivering it from what would destroy it and rescuing it from what has bound it.

The twelve manners toward parents are listed: honoring their dwelling, rising for them, answering their call, lowering one's voice, magnifying and not rebuking them, lowering the wing of humility in mercy, not walking ahead of them in light or darkness, not opposing their command, saying no word of complaint, desiring life for them in old age as they desired it for him in childhood, and providing for their needs as they provided for his.

The twenty-fourth council names three obligatory rights that God will not accept unless discharged in full: the right of God (to come out from what He forbade and enter into what He commanded), the right of parents (thankfulness for what has passed and obedience in what remains), and the right of the child (to be raised with tenderness, nourished, and taught the Book and wisdom); Ali adds that whoever goes against his parents has been undutiful to them.

The nineteenth council divides relatives into twelve categories (children; full brothers, al-ashiqqa'; paternal half-brothers, banu al-'allat; maternal half-brothers, al-akhyaf; paternal grandfathers and grandmothers; maternal grandfathers and grandmothers; paternal uncles and aunts; maternal uncles and aunts), with anyone related through one of these taking that one's ruling, and defines the commanded tie as keeping the bond, giving, drawing near, and loving even when the relatives cut off, withhold, push away, or abandon — and Ali states there is no binding oath in the severing of kinship.

The twentieth council, building on parents and kinship, divides safeguarding the neighbor into seven ranks graded by how many rights each holds — the kin-believer neighbor (neighborliness, kinship, faith), the kin non-believer neighbor (neighborliness, kinship), the believing stranger-neighbor (neighborliness, faith), the companion at your side who differs in religion and creed (neighborliness), the companion aboard ship (right of nearness), the one who shares your litter, and the one who sits with you to receive wisdom, whose sanctity is the most binding of all.

Twelve manners of neighborliness are enumerated — not peering into or eavesdropping on the neighbor's house, not disclosing what one learns of him, not letting him hear or see what he would hate, not withholding a household implement he asks for, not acting haughtily when higher in station nor envying when he is above, helping when he seeks help, covering his 'awrah if exposed, causing him no injury, and bearing his injury with patience — these being called the deeds of a people whose hearts God has tested for piety.
